title: CPCB National Air Quality Index categories
source: Central Pollution Control Board (2014). National Air Quality Index. Control of Urban Pollution Series CUPS/82/2014-15, New Delhi
tags: aqi cpcb categories breakpoints sub-index pm25 pm10 no2 good satisfactory moderate poor severe
content: India's National AQI (launched 2014) has six categories: Good (0-50), Satisfactory (51-100), Moderate (101-200), Poor (201-300), Very Poor (301-400) and Severe (401-500). It covers up to eight pollutants (PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3, Pb). The overall AQI is the highest pollutant sub-index, and is reported only when at least three pollutants are available, one of which must be PM2.5 or PM10. Most pollutants use 24-hour averages; CO and O3 use 8-hour averages.

title: CPCB AQI health statements
source: Central Pollution Control Board (2014). National Air Quality Index. Control of Urban Pollution Series CUPS/82/2014-15, New Delhi (health statements table)
tags: aqi health impact sensitive groups asthma children elderly advisory exposure
content: CPCB associates each AQI category with a health statement. Good: minimal impact. Satisfactory: minor breathing discomfort to sensitive people. Moderate: breathing discomfort to people with lung disease such as asthma, and discomfort to people with heart disease, children and older adults. Poor: breathing discomfort to most people on prolonged exposure. Very Poor: respiratory illness on prolonged exposure. Severe: affects healthy people and seriously impacts those with existing diseases.

title: National Clean Air Programme (NCAP)
source: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (2019). National Clean Air Programme (NCAP). Government of India, New Delhi
tags: ncap clean air programme policy pm reduction city action plan non-attainment mitigation
content: The National Clean Air Programme was launched in January 2019 to reduce particulate matter (PM10/PM2.5) in non-attainment cities through city-specific action plans. Its original goal of a 20-30% reduction relative to 2017 was later revised to up to 40% reduction in PM10 by 2025-26. Mumbai is among the cities covered by NCAP city action plans.

title: Seasonal pattern of Mumbai air quality
source: CPCB (2010). Air Quality Monitoring, Emission Inventory and Source Apportionment Study for Indian Cities (Mumbai study by CSIR-NEERI); CPCB/MPCB CAAQMS records
tags: mumbai aqi season winter monsoon sea breeze inversion mixing height ventilation
content: Mumbai's particulate pollution is typically lowest during the southwest monsoon (June-September), when rain washes out aerosols and strong onshore winds ventilate the city, and highest in winter (roughly November-February), when sea breezes weaken, mixing heights are lower and calm, stable conditions trap emissions near the ground. The same emissions can therefore produce very different AQI values in different seasons.

title: Major particulate sources in Mumbai
source: CPCB (2010). Air Quality Monitoring, Emission Inventory and Source Apportionment Study for Indian Cities (Mumbai, CSIR-NEERI); BMC (2023) air-pollution mitigation guidelines for construction sites
tags: mumbai pollution sources construction dust vehicles waste burning dumping ground industry bmc guidelines
content: Source-apportionment work and municipal air-quality plans for Mumbai identify road and construction dust, vehicle exhaust, industrial and power-sector emissions, open burning of waste (including at dumping grounds) and sea salt as major contributors to particulate matter. In 2023 the BMC issued construction-site dust-control guidelines covering measures such as site barricading, wind-breaking sheets, water sprinkling and covering debris and materials in transit.

title: Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW)
source: Shepard, D. (1968), A two-dimensional interpolation function for irregularly-spaced data
tags: idw interpolation inverse distance weighting stations estimate uncertainty aqi surface
content: IDW estimates a value at an unsampled location as a weighted average of nearby observations, with weights proportional to 1/distance^p (GeoSense uses p = 2, the 4 nearest stations, at least 2 within 15 km). IDW can never produce a value outside the range of the station values, it does not model emission sources between stations, and uncertainty grows with distance from the nearest monitor. Interpolated AQI is an estimate, not a measurement.

title: OpenAQ and CPCB continuous monitoring stations
source: OpenAQ API v3 documentation (docs.openaq.org); CPCB Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS) network
tags: openaq caaqms station monitoring freshness stale data cpcb mpcb latency
content: OpenAQ is an open-data platform that aggregates air-quality measurements from government reference monitors, including India's Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS) operated by CPCB, state boards such as MPCB, and municipal agencies. Data can arrive late or with gaps, so GeoSense accepts only CPCB/MPCB-backed station data no older than 48 hours, excludes future timestamps, and refuses to build an AQI surface when fewer than three stations qualify.

title: NDVI definition
source: Rouse, J.W. et al. (1974). Monitoring vegetation systems in the Great Plains with ERTS. NASA SP-351, 309-317; Tucker, C.J. (1979). Remote Sensing of Environment 8(2), 127-150
tags: ndvi vegetation index nir red sentinel-2 b8 b4 greenness
content: The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index is NDVI = (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red). Healthy green leaves absorb red light for photosynthesis and strongly reflect near-infrared, so NDVI increases with green vegetation amount and vigour. GeoSense computes it from Sentinel-2 band B8 (842 nm) and B4 (665 nm) at 10 m resolution from a cloud-masked median composite.

title: Interpreting NDVI values
source: Tucker, C.J. (1979). Red and photographic infrared linear combinations for monitoring vegetation. Remote Sensing of Environment 8(2), 127-150; NASA Earth Observatory, Measuring Vegetation (NDVI & EVI)
tags: ndvi range interpretation built-up bare sparse dense forest mangrove saturation
content: Typical NDVI ranges: negative values indicate water; roughly 0 to 0.2 indicates bare soil, rock, roads or built-up surfaces; about 0.2 to 0.4 sparse or stressed vegetation and grass; above about 0.5 dense, healthy vegetation such as forest and mangroves. NDVI saturates over very dense canopies and varies with season, so comparisons are most meaningful within the same season.

title: Monsoon greening and NDVI in Mumbai
source: Zhang, X. et al. (2003). Monitoring vegetation phenology using MODIS. Remote Sensing of Environment 84(3), 471-475
tags: ndvi monsoon season greening phenology dry season post-monsoon mumbai
content: In Mumbai, monsoon rain (June-September) produces rapid greening of grasslands, hill slopes and open plots, so post-monsoon composites (September-October) show high NDVI even in places that are bare or brown in the dry season (March-May). A low NDVI cell immediately after the monsoon is therefore a strong indicator of impervious, built-up land rather than seasonal dryness.

title: Sentinel-2 mission
source: European Space Agency, Copernicus Sentinel-2
tags: sentinel-2 esa copernicus msi bands 10 m revisit surface reflectance qa60 cloud mask
content: Sentinel-2 is an ESA Copernicus mission of twin (now three) polar-orbiting satellites carrying the MultiSpectral Instrument with 13 spectral bands at 10, 20 and 60 m. With two satellites the revisit time at the equator is 5 days. GeoSense uses the harmonized Level-2A surface-reflectance collection (COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED) with QA60 cloud and cirrus masking. Cloudy pixels in the composite are NoData, never filled.

title: Modified Normalized Difference Water Index (MNDWI)
source: Xu, H. (2006), International Journal of Remote Sensing 27(14)
tags: mndwi water detection green swir b3 b11 open water mapping urban
content: MNDWI = (Green - SWIR) / (Green + SWIR). Replacing the near-infrared band of McFeeters' NDWI with shortwave infrared suppresses noise from built-up land, which makes it better for mapping open water in cities. GeoSense uses Sentinel-2 B3 and B11 and treats pixels with MNDWI >= 0.15 in connected groups of at least 5 pixels as water.

title: Normalized Difference Chlorophyll Index (NDCI)
source: Mishra, S. & Mishra, D.R. (2012), Remote Sensing of Environment 117
tags: ndci chlorophyll algae algal bloom eutrophication red edge b5 proxy
content: NDCI = (R705 - R665) / (R705 + R665), using the red-edge band (Sentinel-2 B5) and red band (B4). It was developed as a proxy for chlorophyll-a in turbid, productive coastal and inland waters. Higher NDCI is associated with more algal pigment. Without in-situ calibration it is a relative indicator, not a chlorophyll concentration in mg/m3.

title: Optical turbidity / suspended-sediment proxy
source: Dogliotti, A.I. et al. (2015). A single algorithm to retrieve turbidity from remotely-sensed data in all coastal and estuarine waters. Remote Sensing of Environment 156, 157-168
tags: turbidity suspended sediment proxy red reflectance ntu calibration limitations
content: Reflectance in the red band rises as suspended sediment and turbidity increase, so green-red band ratios provide a relative turbidity proxy. Satellite proxies cannot be reported in NTU or mg/L without matched field samples, and they can be confused by shallow bottoms, floating vegetation, glint or adjacency to bright land.

title: GeoSense Water Health index
source: GeoSense methodology (this project): MNDWI water mask (Xu 2006), NDCI (Mishra & Mishra 2012), turbidity proxy (Dogliotti et al. 2015)
tags: water health index geosense mndwi ndci turbidity proxy limitations not laboratory
content: GeoSense Water Health is a 0-1 satellite-derived condition indicator computed only for pixels detected as water (MNDWI). It combines an algal-related NDCI-style proxy and a turbidity proxy so that higher values mean less optical stress. Non-water pixels are NoData. It is not a laboratory measurement of dissolved oxygen, BOD, coliforms or toxins, and statistical relationships with it are associations, not causal proof.

title: In-situ water quality monitoring
source: CPCB National Water Quality Monitoring Programme (NWMP); CPCB designated-best-use water quality criteria
tags: water quality monitoring bod dissolved oxygen coliform sampling mpcb validation in-situ
content: Regulatory water quality in India is assessed from field samples under the National Water Quality Monitoring Programme, using parameters such as dissolved oxygen, biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), pH and faecal coliforms. Satellite water-condition proxies are useful for screening where to look, but any concern they raise should be confirmed with sampling by MPCB or the municipal corporation.

title: Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 Surface Temperature
source: USGS Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 Science Products
tags: landsat lst surface temperature tirs band 10 collection 2 level-2 30 m 100 m thermal cloud
content: Landsat 8 (launched 2013) and Landsat 9 (2021) carry the Thermal Infrared Sensor. The Collection 2 Level-2 surface temperature band (ST_B10) is converted to Kelvin with scale 0.00341802 and offset 149.0. The thermal data are collected at 100 m and delivered resampled to 30 m, so GeoSense labels LST as 30 m and never as 10 m. Clouds and cloud shadows corrupt LST; GeoSense treats values below 20 °C over Mumbai as probable residual cloud: hidden in maps and excluded from cell statistics.

title: Land surface temperature vs air temperature
source: Voogt, J.A. & Oke, T.R. (2003). Thermal remote sensing of urban climates. Remote Sensing of Environment 86(3), 370-384
tags: lst skin temperature air temperature overpass roofs pavement thermal remote sensing
content: LST is the radiative 'skin' temperature of roofs, roads, soil and canopy at the satellite overpass time (late morning for Landsat), not the air temperature people feel. On clear days dark roofs and paved surfaces can be much hotter than the air above them, while vegetated and wet surfaces stay close to air temperature. LST maps show where surfaces store and emit heat.

title: Surface urban heat island
source: Oke, T.R. (1982). The energetic basis of the urban heat island. Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society 108(455), 1-24; Voogt & Oke (2003)
tags: urban heat island uhi impervious albedo evapotranspiration built-up density anthropogenic heat
content: The surface urban heat island is the tendency of dense urban areas to have warmer surfaces than vegetated or rural surroundings. Contributors include impervious, low-albedo materials that absorb solar radiation, loss of vegetation and therefore evapotranspiration and shade, reduced airflow in dense building fabric, and waste heat from vehicles, industry and air conditioning.

title: Cooling effect of vegetation
source: Bowler, D.E., Buyung-Ali, L., Knight, T.M. & Pullin, A.S. (2010). Urban greening to cool towns and cities: a systematic review of the empirical evidence. Landscape and Urban Planning 97(3), 147-155
tags: vegetation trees cooling evapotranspiration shade park green space ndvi lst
content: Trees and other vegetation cool their surroundings through evapotranspiration and shading. Parks and forest patches generally show markedly lower surface temperatures than nearby built-up blocks, and the cooling extends some distance into adjacent streets. In GeoSense's XGBoost model, dense-vegetation share and NDVI typically lower the expected LST of a cell.

title: Cooling effect of water and the sea breeze
source: Völker, S. et al. (2013). Evidence for the temperature-mitigating capacity of urban blue space - a health geographic perspective. Erdkunde 67(4), 355-371
tags: water cooling sea breeze coast lake creek distance heat capacity
content: Water bodies have high heat capacity and evaporative cooling, so lakes, creeks and the sea have lower daytime surface temperature than land. In a coastal city like Mumbai the afternoon sea breeze also moderates temperatures near the shore. Distance to open water is therefore a meaningful predictor of surface heat.

title: Mumbai's post-monsoon 'October heat'
source: India Meteorological Department, Climatological Normals 1991-2020 (Mumbai Santacruz and Colaba)
tags: october heat post-monsoon withdrawal humidity temperature mumbai imd
content: After the southwest monsoon withdraws from Mumbai, usually in early October, skies clear while humidity stays high. Daytime temperatures commonly rise again in October, a period locals call 'October heat', before cooler winter air arrives in November-December. Landsat scenes from October therefore often show strong urban surface heat contrasts.

title: Mumbai climate
source: India Meteorological Department, Climatological Normals 1991-2020 (Mumbai Santacruz and Colaba)
tags: mumbai climate monsoon rainfall tropical cloud cover satellite gaps
content: Mumbai has a tropical wet-and-dry climate. Almost all of its annual rainfall, typically over 2,000 mm, falls during the southwest monsoon from June to September. Persistent monsoon cloud makes optical and thermal satellite observations scarce in those months, which is why GeoSense leaves cloudy pixels as NoData instead of filling them.

title: Mumbai Climate Action Plan (MCAP)
source: Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, Mumbai Climate Action Plan (2022)
tags: mumbai climate action plan mcap bmc net zero 2050 greening heat flooding policy
content: The BMC released the Mumbai Climate Action Plan in March 2022, targeting net-zero emissions by 2050. It covers urban greening and biodiversity, urban flooding and water resource management, sustainable mobility, air quality, energy and buildings, and waste management, and identifies urban heat and flooding as key climate risks for the city.

title: Sanjay Gandhi National Park
source: Maharashtra Forest Department
tags: sgnp sanjay gandhi national park forest vihar tulsi lake borivali green cool
content: Sanjay Gandhi National Park covers roughly 100 km2 of forested hills in the middle of the Mumbai-Thane urban area. It contains the Vihar and Tulsi lakes, which supply drinking water to Mumbai, and the Kanheri Caves. It is the largest green and cool area in the study region and appears as high NDVI and low LST.

title: Thane Creek and the Flamingo Sanctuary
source: Maharashtra Mangrove Cell; Ramsar Convention
tags: thane creek flamingo sanctuary ramsar mangroves mudflats wetland wastewater
content: Thane Creek separates Mumbai's eastern suburbs and Thane from Navi Mumbai. Its mudflats and mangroves host large flocks of flamingos in winter. The Thane Creek Flamingo Sanctuary was notified in 2015 and designated a Ramsar wetland of international importance in 2022. The creek receives urban and industrial wastewater, so water-condition signals here are relevant to wetland health.

title: Mangroves of the Mumbai region
source: Maharashtra Mangrove Cell; Bombay High Court (2018)
tags: mangroves creek wetland flooding buffer carbon protection high court ndvi
content: Mangrove forests line Mumbai's creeks, including Thane Creek, Mahim, Malad-Marve, Manori-Gorai and Vasai Creek near Mira-Bhayandar. They buffer storm surge and flooding, store carbon, support fisheries and appear as high-NDVI wetland vegetation. A 2018 Bombay High Court judgment ordered protection of mangroves across Maharashtra, including a buffer zone around them.

title: Mithi River
source: Mithi River Development and Protection Authority; MPCB
tags: mithi river pollution sewage kurla bkc mahim creek flood 2005 encroachment
content: The Mithi River rises near the Vihar and Powai lakes and flows about 18 km through Powai, Saki Naka, Kurla and Bandra-Kurla Complex into Mahim Creek. It receives untreated sewage, industrial effluent and solid waste along its course and has been narrowed by encroachment. After the 26 July 2005 deluge, when Santacruz recorded about 944 mm of rain in 24 hours, the state created the Mithi River Development and Protection Authority.

title: Powai Lake
source: Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (lake authority); MPCB water-quality monitoring
tags: powai lake eutrophication water hyacinth sewage nutrient
content: Powai Lake is an artificial lake created in the late nineteenth century in the eastern suburbs of Mumbai. Its water is no longer used for drinking supply. Sewage inflow from surrounding settlements has caused nutrient enrichment and recurring growth of water hyacinth, which can affect optical water-condition signals.

title: Thane's lakes
source: Thane Municipal Corporation
tags: thane lakes masunda upvan urban lake pollution immersion
content: Thane is often called the 'city of lakes' because it has dozens of urban lakes, such as Masunda (Talao Pali) and Upvan. Many are affected by sewage inflow, idol immersion and encroachment; they are visible in GeoSense as small detected-water bodies with Water Health values.

title: Mira-Bhayandar setting
source: Mira-Bhayandar Municipal Corporation; Census of India (2011)
tags: mira bhayandar vasai creek salt pans wetlands mangroves urban growth
content: Mira-Bhayandar lies north of Mumbai's Dahisar, bounded by Vasai Creek to the north and by creeks, salt pans and mangrove wetlands to the west. Large wetland and salt-pan areas mean open water, mudflat and mangrove signals are common in its cells, alongside rapidly built-up urban land.

title: Isolation Forest anomaly detection
source: Liu, F.T., Ting, K.M. & Zhou, Z.-H. (2008). Isolation Forest. IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM), 413-422
tags: isolation forest anomaly detection unsupervised outlier score contamination random trees
content: Isolation Forest detects anomalies by building random trees that split features at random values; points with unusual feature combinations are isolated in fewer splits and receive higher anomaly scores. It is unsupervised: an 'anomaly' means statistically unusual relative to the other cells in the snapshot, not necessarily harmful. GeoSense standardises the features and sets contamination to 5%. In GeoSense it is run on land cells only (cells under 50% open water), using shares of the cell's land area, so shoreline and water cells are not flagged just for being rare; water cells are assessed separately with the Water Health robust z-score.

title: XGBoost and TreeSHAP contributions
source: Chen, T. & Guestrin, C. (2016). XGBoost: A scalable tree boosting system. KDD '16, 785-794; Lundberg, S.M. et al. (2020). From local explanations to global understanding with explainable AI for trees. Nature Machine Intelligence 2, 56-67
tags: xgboost gradient boosting shap contributions attribution feature importance explanation
content: XGBoost is a gradient-boosted decision-tree method. GeoSense uses it to predict a cell's land surface temperature from land-cover features. TreeSHAP contributions split each prediction into a baseline plus a signed contribution (in °C) from every feature, so the panel can say, for example, that a high built-up share raised expected LST. These are model attributions, not physical proof.

title: Spatial cross-validation
source: Roberts, D.R. et al. (2017). Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography 40(8), 913-929
tags: spatial cross validation autocorrelation blocks overfitting residual out-of-fold
content: Nearby cells are similar (spatial autocorrelation), so ordinary random cross-validation overstates model skill. GeoSense evaluates the LST model with blocked cross-validation on about 3 km spatial blocks and uses out-of-fold predictions to compute residuals, so 'unexplained heat' is not an artefact of the model memorising its training cell.

title: Interpreting LST model residuals
source: GeoSense methodology (this project); interpretation follows Roberts et al. (2017), Ecography 40, 913-929
tags: residual unexplained heat cooling expected lst roofs industrial albedo flagged
content: A positive residual means a cell is hotter than its vegetation, water and built-up share would predict; possible associated factors include dark roofs, industrial or transport surfaces, low wind exposure or materials with low albedo. A negative residual means it is cooler than expected, for example due to shade, irrigation, wetland or sea-breeze exposure. Residuals larger than twice the cross-validated RMSE are flagged.

title: Robust z-score (median/MAD)
source: Iglewicz & Hoaglin (1993), How to Detect and Handle Outliers
tags: robust z score median mad outlier water health baseline
content: A robust z-score uses the median and the median absolute deviation (MAD, scaled by 1.4826) instead of the mean and standard deviation, so a few extreme values do not distort the baseline. GeoSense flags water cells whose Water Health index is more than 2 robust standard deviations below the median of all water cells.

title: Pixel, cell and municipality in GeoSense
source: GeoSense architecture (this project)
tags: pixel cell municipality 300 m grid architecture geotiff resolution
content: GeoSense reports three different levels. The pixel is the exact value from the scientific GeoTIFF at the clicked location (10 m for Sentinel-2, 30 m for Landsat). The cell is a 300 m analytical grid square used for aggregation and machine learning. The municipality (Mumbai, Thane or Mira-Bhayandar) is administrative context only. Smoothed heatmaps are visual; clicked values always come from the original raster.

title: Cloud gaps and NoData
source: GeoSense data policy (this project); USGS Landsat Collection 2 QA guidance
tags: cloud nodata missing gaps no imputation data policy
content: Optical and thermal satellites cannot see through clouds. GeoSense keeps cloudy or invalid pixels as NoData and excludes cells with too few clear pixels from statistics and models, rather than filling them with neighbouring or historical values. A missing value means 'not observed', never zero.

title: Reducing urban surface heat
source: NDMA (2019). National Guidelines for Preparation of Action Plan - Prevention and Management of Heat Wave; Santamouris, M. (2014). Cooling the cities. Solar Energy 103, 682-703
tags: heat mitigation cool roofs trees green roofs albedo paving heat action plan ndma
content: Evidence-based measures to lower surface heat include cool or reflective roofs (high-albedo coatings), shade trees along streets, green roofs and pocket parks, permeable and lighter-coloured paving, protecting existing water bodies and wetlands, and keeping open space for ventilation. Heat action plans also include early warnings and cooling access for vulnerable residents.

title: Reducing particulate pollution in cities
source: MoEFCC (2019). National Clean Air Programme; BMC (2023) air-pollution mitigation guidelines for construction sites
tags: air pollution mitigation dust control road sweeping waste burning electric buses exposure
content: Common city measures to reduce particulate matter include enforcing construction-dust controls, mechanised road sweeping and water sprinkling, paving unpaved shoulders, stopping open waste burning and landfill fires, shifting buses and fleets to electric or cleaner fuels, and controlling industrial emissions. Residents can reduce exposure on Poor or worse days by limiting outdoor exertion.

title: Improving urban water bodies
source: MoEFCC National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA); CPCB National Water Quality Monitoring Programme
tags: water restoration sewage treatment hyacinth dumping buffer mangrove monitoring lake river
content: Measures to improve urban lakes, rivers and creeks include intercepting and treating sewage before it enters the water body, preventing solid-waste dumping and encroachment, removing invasive water hyacinth, restoring vegetated and mangrove buffers, and regular in-situ monitoring of DO, BOD and coliforms to confirm satellite signals.

title: Protecting and adding vegetation
source: Bowler, D.E. et al. (2010). Landscape and Urban Planning 97(3), 147-155; BMC (2022). Mumbai Climate Action Plan
tags: greening trees plantation mangrove protection urban forest native species miyawaki
content: Protecting forests, mangroves and existing tree cover is usually more effective than new planting. Where vegetation is sparse, street trees, native-species plantations, Miyawaki-style dense plantations on open plots, and greening of school and institutional campuses can raise NDVI and provide shade and cooling over time.

title: Per-layer Isolation Forest in GeoSense
source: Liu, F.T., Ting, K.M. & Zhou, Z.-H. (2008), IEEE ICDM; GeoSense methodology
tags: isolation forest anomaly ndvi lst water health aqi local contrast hotspot
content: Besides the combined (multivariate) Isolation Forest, GeoSense trains one Isolation Forest per map layer: NDVI, LST, Water Health and interpolated AQI. Each uses three kinds of evidence for a 300 m cell: its value, its within-cell variability, and its contrast with the surrounding 1 km (the cell value minus the mean of neighbouring cells). A cell can therefore be flagged as unusually high, unusually low, or as an unusual pattern (for example a sharp local hotspot or a very patchy cell) for that layer. About 5% of cells per layer are flagged. Flags are statistical: they point to where to look, not to a cause. For the AQI layer only the interpolated value is used: between stations AQI is an IDW estimate, so local contrast would mostly reflect interpolation seams rather than real pollution differences; the station-level Isolation Forest is the stronger AQI anomaly signal.

title: Station-level Isolation Forest for air quality
source: Liu, F.T., Ting, K.M. & Zhou, Z.-H. (2008), IEEE ICDM; CPCB National AQI (2014)
tags: isolation forest aqi station pollutant pm2.5 pm10 no2 sub-index
content: Interpolated AQI is smooth between stations, so GeoSense also runs an Isolation Forest on the real monitoring stations themselves, using each station's CPCB pollutant sub-indices (PM2.5, PM10, NO2, SO2, O3, CO where reported). A flagged station has a pollutant mix unlike the other stations, for example much higher NO2 relative to particulates, which is often associated with traffic, or unusually high PM10, often associated with dust or construction. Stations missing a commonly reported pollutant are left out rather than filled in.

title: Typical sources associated with each CPCB pollutant
source: CPCB National Air Quality Index (2014); WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021)
tags: no2 pm10 pm2.5 so2 o3 ozone co sources traffic dust combustion industry dominant pollutant
content: Each pollutant in the CPCB AQI has typical source associations. NO2 is mainly associated with traffic and other fuel combustion. PM10 is associated with road and construction dust and re-suspended particles. PM2.5 is associated with combustion sources such as vehicles, industry and open waste burning. SO2 is associated with industrial and fuel-oil combustion. O3 (ozone) is a secondary pollutant formed in sunlight from NOx and VOC emissions, so it is often higher away from busy roads. CO is associated with incomplete combustion. A station's dominant pollutant is a clue to likely source types, not proof of a specific source.
